Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones
Medical equipment such as needles or drips

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try to push them out of my mind

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: I acted in ways that go against who I am
I have permanently changed for the worse
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Weapons): Weapons or objects used as weapons
issues.explanation: For trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness, weapon-related visual triggers are hard to reconcile unless there is additional unreported violent trauma. Hospital smells and loss-related conversations fit, but weapons/object-as-weapon cues are clinically implausible for the same index trauma.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'You can never know who will harm you' implies interpersonal danger/assailant threat, which is poorly matched to the validated trauma of a child's serious illness. This also aligns awkwardly with the rest of the profile, which is otherwise illness/loss/moral injury themed rather than assault-based.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: 'Intense rage on recall' is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile for an 80-year-old mother traumatized by a child's life-threatening illness. The other items center on helplessness, permanent change, loss-related and hospital triggers, and intrusive affect without image. Distress, fear, guilt, grief, or sadness would fit more coherently; rage is not impossible, but here it is insufficiently supported by any corresponding appraisal or trigger content and stands out as clinically incongruent.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Face Hiding: cover face with hands
issues.explanation: 'Cover face with hands' is not well supported as a maladaptive strategy in this profile. The active formulation links maladaptive strategies mainly to negative appraisals and memory, and the other strategies chosen (avoid going out, thought suppression) fit intrusive distress and negative beliefs. Face hiding is more typical of acute shame/panic/social exposure and is not clearly connected to the hospital/loss triggers, intrusive memory pattern, or appraisals provided, making it the least coherent item in this set.

vignette:
Zahra's Vigil

Zahra was eighty years old when she came to the clinic, her silver hair pinned back with the same careful precision she had maintained for sixty years, her hands folded in her lap with the composure of someone who had spent a lifetime holding other people's crises at arm's length. She had been a social worker for nearly five decades, the kind of woman who sat across from families in their worst moments and helped them find the next step. Now, at eighty, she could barely leave her apartment.

Thirty-two years ago, her son Reza had fallen ill. He was seven years old, bright-eyed and full of the kind of restless energy that drove her to distraction in the best way. One autumn morning he complained of a sore throat. By evening, his fever had climbed to 104. By the next morning, he was struggling to breathe. The hospital admitted him within hours, and what should have been a simple case of epiglottitis became a three-week ordeal that nearly took his life. Zahra remembered the moment the pediatrician pulled her aside in that fluorescent hallway, the smell of antiseptic and something else—something organic and wrong—filling her nostrils as he explained that Reza might need to be intubated. She remembered the needle going into his small arm for the IV line, the way his eyes found hers as if asking her to make it stop. She had held his hand and promised him it would be all right. She had lied.

Reza survived. He recovered fully, went on to university, to a career, to a family of his own. But something in Zahra had not recovered from those three weeks. For years she had managed it well enough. She continued her work, helped her clients navigate their own traumas, raised her other children, built a life with her late husband Kaveh. But as she aged, as Kaveh died five years ago, as the world seemed to grow smaller and more fragile around her, the weight of what she had lived through began to surface in ways she could not control.

It started with conversations. When a colleague mentioned her sister's cancer diagnosis, Zahra felt the ground tilt beneath her. When her granddaughter spoke casually about a friend whose mother had passed away, Zahra found herself unable to breathe normally for the rest of the afternoon. She had come to understand that hearing about anyone's loss—anyone's child sick, anyone's loved one dying—was a trigger she could not manage. The talk of loss seemed to pull at something fundamental in her, a thread that unraveled into panic and grief so overwhelming it surprised her with its ferocity.

She began to avoid going out. First it was just the social events she had always attended—the weekly gatherings with her women's group, the neighborhood walks she had loved. Then it was the grocery store, because you never knew who you might run into or what they might tell you. Her daughter-in-law had gently suggested a doctor's appointment for her blood pressure, and Zahra had found herself unable to go. The thought of sitting in a waiting room, of a nurse approaching with a blood pressure cuff, of that clinical smell—the same smell that had haunted her in the hospital all those years ago—made her chest tight and her mind blank with refusal.

The memory itself had changed over the decades. Sometimes she would be sitting quietly, doing nothing in particular, and suddenly she would feel the full weight of her terror and helplessness, though the images of that hospital room would not come. The emotion would arrive unannounced and complete, as if her body remembered what her mind had tried to forget. Other times, unbidden, the memory would force itself into her consciousness—Reza's pale face, the sound of the monitors, the terrible helplessness of watching your child suffer and being unable to stop it. When it came, it brought grief so profound that she would sit in her bedroom for hours afterward, unable to do anything but sit.

What frightened her most was the conviction that had settled into her bones: she had failed him. She had promised to protect him and she could not. She had acted against everything she believed in—she had abandoned her composure, her professional distance, her faith in her own competence—and in doing so, she had become someone she no longer recognized. The worst part was knowing that she could not have stopped it. She was eighty years old and she still could not accept that some things simply happen, that no amount of vigilance or love or sacrifice can prevent suffering. She had spent her life helping others come to terms with exactly this truth, and she could not apply it to herself.

Her daughter had finally insisted she see someone. Zahra sat in the clinic waiting room, avoiding the antiseptic-scented hand sanitizer by the door, and wondered if at eighty, after three decades of carrying this, there was any point in trying to change.
